41	       \oplus(L_1\otimes L_2)^{\oplus j}.
42	\]

44	\(w_1(L_1)=x\) and \(w_1(L_2)=y\). The Whitney product formula gives
45	\[
46	w_{3j}(E)=x^jy^j(x+y)^j.
47	\]

54	\]

59	F_{2,i}(u,v)&=\int\operatorname{sgn}(\ell_v)\,d\mu_i,\\
60	F_{3,i}(u,v)&=\int\operatorname{sgn}(\ell_u)
61	                         \operatorname{sgn}(\ell_v)\,d\mu_i .
62	\end{aligned}
63	\]
64	Absolute continuity and dominated convergence give continuity, including at the two parameters representing constant affine functions. The transformation rules are exactly those of the zero lemma.
65

67	\[

69	                 +\eta F_{2,i}+\varepsilon\eta F_{3,i}\right)=\frac14.
70	\tag{2}
71	\]

78	\]

97	## 2. An algebraic construction for the lower bound

102	\[
103	x^TA_ry=0\quad\text{for every }r
104	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=0\ \text{or}\ y=0.
105	\tag{4}
106	\]
107	
108	### Proof
109	
110	Put \(n=2m\), where \(m\ge2\), and identify \(\mathbb R^{2m}\) with the complex polynomials of degree at most \(m-1\), using coefficient vectors.
111	
112	Let
113	\[
114	p(t)=\prod_{r=1}^{2m-2}(t+r).
115	\]
116	For each partition of its roots into two sets of size \(m-1\), write
117	\[
118	p=u\,v
119	\]
120	with \(u,v\) monic. Their coefficient vectors are positive, and \(u,v\) are linearly independent.
121	
122	Choose a real skew-symmetric matrix \(K\) such that
123	\[
124	u^TKv\ne0
125	\tag{5}
126	\]
127	for every such complementary pair. Such a \(K\) exists: for each pair, \(u^TKv=0\) is a proper linear hyperplane in the space of skew-symmetric matrices, because \(u,v\) are independent. A finite union of proper hyperplanes cannot cover that space.
128	
129	Here is also an explicit integer choice, useful for computation. All factor coefficients are at most
130	\[
131	C=(2m-1)!.
132	\]
133	Enumerate the pairs \(a<b\) by distinct exponents \(e(a,b)=0,1,\ldots\), choose
134	\[
135	T=4C^2+2,\qquad K_{ab}=T^{e(a,b)},\quad K_{ba}=-K_{ab}.
136	\]
137	Then \(u^TKv\) is a nonzero integer polynomial evaluated at \(T\), with coefficients bounded in absolute value by \(2C^2\). Its leading term dominates all the others, proving (5).
138	
139	For complex coefficient vectors \(f,g\), consider the following real bilinear forms:
140	
141	* the real and imaginary parts of all \(2m-2\) coefficients of
142	  \(fg\bmod p\);
143	* \(\operatorname{Re}(f^*g)\);
144	* \(\operatorname{Re}(i f^*Kg)\).
145	
146	There are
147	\[
148	2(2m-2)+2=4m-2=2n-2
149	\]
150	forms. They are symmetric as real bilinear forms; for the last one, this follows because \(iK\) is Hermitian.
151	
152	We claim that they have no common zero with \(f,g\ne0\).
153	
154	If all remainder coefficients vanish, then \(p\mid fg\). The degree bounds force
155	\[
156	fg=c\,p,\qquad
157	f=\alpha u,\quad g=\beta v,
158	\]
159	for one of the complementary monic factor pairs above and nonzero complex numbers \(\alpha,\beta\).
160	
161	Set \(\gamma=\overline\alpha\beta\). The last two equations become
162	\[
163	(u^Tv)\operatorname{Re}\gamma=0,\qquad
164	-(u^TKv)\operatorname{Im}\gamma=0.
165	\]
166	Here \(u^Tv>0\), and (5) holds. Thus \(\gamma=0\), a contradiction.
167	
168	Write these real symmetric forms as \(x^TS_ry\). One of the \(S_r\) is \(I\). Keep that matrix, and replace every other \(S_r\) by
169	\[
170	A_r=S_r+\lambda I
171	\]
172	with \(\lambda\) sufficiently large to make it positive definite. A common zero of the new forms has \(x^Ty=0\), and hence is also a common zero of all the original forms. This proves (4). ∎
173	
174	## 3. Gaussian counterexamples in dimension \(3n-3\)
175	
176	Apply the lemma, with
177	\[
178	j=2n-2,\qquad d_0=(j-1)+n=3n-3.
179	\]
180	
181	Decompose
182	\[
183	\mathbb R^{d_0}=\mathbb R^{j-1}\oplus\mathbb R^n.
184	\]
185	Choose \(j\) Gaussian probability measures with respective means
186	\[
187	0,e_1,\ldots,e_{j-1}
188	\]
189	and covariance matrices
190	\[
191	\Sigma_r=
192	\begin{pmatrix}
193	I_{j-1}&0\\
194	0&A_r
195	\end{pmatrix}.
196	\]
197	All these measures have everywhere-positive Lebesgue densities.
198	
199	Suppose two hyperplanes quarter every one of these measures. Each hyperplane must bisect every measure. A hyperplane bisects a nondegenerate Gaussian exactly when it contains its mean. Thus both hyperplanes contain
200	\[
201	\mathbb R^{j-1}\oplus\{0\}.
202	\]
203	Their equations therefore have the form
204	\[
205	x^Tz=0,\qquad y^Tz=0
206	\]
207	for nonzero \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\).
208	
209	For the \(r\)-th Gaussian, the two defining linear functions are jointly centered Gaussian, with covariance
210	\[
211	x^TA_ry.
212	\]
213	For centered jointly Gaussian variables of correlation \(\rho\),
214	\[
215	\Pr(X>0,Y>0)=\frac14+\frac{\arcsin\rho}{2\pi}.
216	\tag{6}
217	\]
218	This follows, for example, by representing them as two linear functions of a rotationally invariant planar Gaussian and measuring the corresponding angular sector. In particular, quartering forces their covariance to be zero.
219	
220	We obtain
221	\[
222	x^TA_ry=0\qquad(r=1,\ldots,j),
223	\]
224	contradicting (4). So dimension \(3n-3\) does not work.
225	
226	Finally, the desired property is monotone in dimension: push measures forward under a coordinate projection, find the hyperplanes in the smaller space, and lift them. Absolute continuity of the pushforwards follows from Fubini's theorem. Thus failure in dimension \(3n-3\) rules out every smaller dimension as well, giving
227	\[
228	D_s\ge3n-2.
229	\tag{7}
230	\]
231	Combining (3) and (7) proves the answer.
232	
233	## 4. Exact computational checks
234	
235	The following Python uses integer and symbolic arithmetic, not numerical sampling. It constructs the matrices and checks:
236	
237	* the polynomial-remainder identities defining every bilinear form;
238	* positive definiteness by strict diagonal dominance;
239	* the change from the original forms to positive-definite forms;
240	* all complementary factor pairs for the tested cases;
241	* the affine-bisector constraints on the Gaussian means;
242	* the complete surviving mod-\(2\) obstruction polynomial.
243	
244	The argument above proves all parameters; the computations give exact certificates for \(s=3,4,5\).

248	from itertools import combinations
249	import sympy as S
250	
251	
252	def mul(a, b):
253	    c = [0] * (len(a) + len(b) - 1)
254	    for i, x in enumerate(a):
255	        for k, y in enumerate(b):
256	            c[i + k] += x * y
257	    return c
258	
259	
260	def factor_vector(roots):
261	    a = [1]
262	    for r in roots:
263	        a = mul(a, [r, 1])
264	    return a
265	
266

268	    assert s >= 3
269	    m = 2**(s - 2)
270	    n, j = 2*m, 4*m - 2
271	    d0, d = 6*m - 3, 6*m - 2
272	
273	    roots = tuple(range(1, 2*m - 1))

275	    C = factorial(2*m - 1)
276	    T = 4*C*C + 2
277	
278	    K = S.zeros(m)
279	    exponent = 0
280	    for a in range(m):
281	        for b in range(a + 1, m):
282	            K[a, b] = T**exponent
283	            K[b, a] = -T**exponent
284	            exponent += 1

286	
287	    # R[k] gives coefficient k of f*g modulo p.
288	    R = []
289	    for k in range(2*m - 2):
290	        R.append(S.Matrix(
291	            m, m,
292	            lambda a, b:
293	                int(a + b == k) if a + b < 2*m - 2 else -p[k]
294	        ))
295	
296	    t = S.Symbol("t")
297	    P = sum(c*t**a for a, c in enumerate(p))
298	
299	    # Checking on basis monomials certifies the full bilinear identity.
300	    for a in range(m):
301	        for b in range(m):
302	            rhs = sum(R[k][a, b]*t**k for k in range(2*m - 2))
303	            assert S.rem(t**(a + b) - rhs, P, t) == 0
304	
305	    Z = S.zeros(m)
306	    B = []
307	    for r in R:
308	        B.extend([
309	            S.BlockMatrix([[r, Z], [Z, -r]]).as_explicit(),
310	            S.BlockMatrix([[Z, r], [r, Z]]).as_explicit()
311	        ])
312	
313	    I = S.eye(n)
314	    B.extend([
315	        I,
316	        S.BlockMatrix([[Z, -K], [K, Z]]).as_explicit()
317	    ])
318	    assert len(B) == j
319	    assert all(b == b.T for b in B)
320	
321	    identity_index = j - 2
322	    M = 1 + max(
323	        sum(abs(b[a, c]) for c in range(n))
324	        for b in B for a in range(n)
325	    )
326	    A = [
327	        I if k == identity_index else M*I + b
328	        for k, b in enumerate(B)
329	    ]
330	
331	    for k, a in enumerate(A):
332	        assert a == a.T
333	        # Positive diagonal + strict diagonal dominance => positive definite.
334	        assert all(
335	            a[r, r] >
336	            sum(abs(a[r, c]) for c in range(n) if c != r)
337	            for r in range(n)
338	        )
339	        if k == identity_index:
340	            assert a == I
341	        else:
342	            assert a - M*A[identity_index] == B[k]
343	
344	    # Bisector equations for means 0,e_1,...,e_{j-1}.
345	    # Columns: offset, first j-1 normal entries, final n entries.
346	    E = S.zeros(j, d0 + 1)
347	    for r in range(j):
348	        E[r, 0] = -1
349	    for r in range(1, j):
350	        E[r, r] = 1
351	    assert E[:, :j].det() != 0
352	    assert E[:, j:] == S.zeros(j, n)
353	
354	    checked = 0
355	    if exhaustive:
356	        for subset in combinations(roots, m - 1):
357	            # One representative per unordered factor pair.
358	            if 1 not in subset:
359	                continue
360	            complement = tuple(r for r in roots if r not in subset)
361	            u = S.Matrix(factor_vector(subset))
362	            v = S.Matrix(factor_vector(complement))
363	
364	            assert mul(list(u), list(v)) == p
365	            assert all(0 < a <= C for a in list(u) + list(v))
366	            assert u.dot(v) > 0
367	
368	            wedge = [
369	                u[a]*v[b] - u[b]*v[a]
370	                for a in range(m) for b in range(a + 1, m)
371	            ]
372	            assert any(wedge)
373	            assert max(map(abs, wedge)) <= 2*C*C
374	            assert (u.T*K*v)[0] != 0
375	            assert all((u.T*r*v)[0] == 0 for r in R)
376	
377	            # Determinant of the two equations on Re(gamma), Im(gamma).
378	            assert u.dot(v) * (u.T*K*v)[0] != 0
379	            checked += 1
380	
381	        assert checked == comb(2*m - 2, m - 1)//2
382	
383	    # Compute all terms of x^j*y^j*(x+y)^j modulo 2,
384	    # then quotient by x^(d+1), y^(d+1).
385	    monomials = {
386	        (j + k, 2*j - k)
387	        for k in range(j + 1) if comb(j, k) % 2
388	    }
389	    surviving = {
390	        (a, b) for a, b in monomials if a <= d and b <= d
391	    }
392	    assert (3*n - 2, 3*n - 4) in surviving

394	    print(
395	        f"s={s}: lower counterexample dimension {d0}; upper {d}; "
396	        f"factor pairs certified {checked}; "
397	        f"surviving monomials {sorted(surviving)}"
398	    )
